claims.text: Selective dealloying of a pre-synthesized noble metal–based high-entropy alloy can produce three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Less-noble elements can be preferentially dissolved from an NM-HEA.
Preferential dissolution yields an interconnected, noble-metal-rich porous structure.
The resulting porous structure has enhanced catalytic surface area.
The proposed starting material is a bulk NM-HEA containing both noble and less-noble metallic components.
Chemical acid or alkaline etching can selectively remove less-noble elements.
Controlling temperature, etchant concentration, and processing time can balance selective dissolution against framework integrity.
Noble and less-noble elements exhibit differential electrochemical dissolution rates.
Differential dissolution produces voids in the alloy.
Residual noble atoms reorganize into a three-dimensional interconnected nanostructure during dealloying.
Selective removal of less-noble species reduces local atomic density.
Reduced local atomic density instigates self-assembly of the remaining noble atoms into a high-surface-area nanoframework.
The high-surface-area nanoframework provides abundant catalytically active sites.
Dealloying will form a three-dimensional porous nanoframework.
The dealloyed material will have significantly greater surface area than the original bulk alloy.
The dealloyed material will have enhanced catalytic activity relative to the original bulk alloy.
The untreated NM-HEA is more homogeneous, less porous, and has lower catalytic surface accessibility than the proposed dealloyed material.
Selective dealloying requires sufficiently different elemental nobility or dissolution behavior.
If all alloying elements have similar dissolution behavior, dealloying may not produce a well-defined porous framework.
Optimal etchant type, concentration, treatment time, temperature, pore size, and connectivity require experimental validation.
